accepted.question_text: Within the paper's standard ansatz for classical de Sitter solutions in 10d type II supergravity - namely a 10d metric globally written as a 4d de Sitter space-time times a 6d compact manifold, with Op/Dp sources, then further restricted to smeared solutions on 6d compact group manifolds with constant fluxes - is there any classical de Sitter solution whose sources are parallel, meaning that the sources lie along the same dimensions in the 10d space-time, or must every such putative solution be excluded?

evidence.quote: The understanding of these solutions, built from all these works, has led to general beliefs that we formulate below as conjectures. Proving (or disproving) these conjectures has remained so far open problems, on which we report here.

We express them generally, but have in mind in this paper to (dis)prove them for the ansatz just discussed, i.e. for smeared solutions on group manifolds with constant fluxes, for which at least the question mathematically well-defined.
Conjecture 1 There is no classical de Sitter solution with parallel sources.

accepted.question_text: For classical de Sitter solutions in the same standard type-II-supergravity ansatz, must every solution with intersecting Op/Dp sources be perturbatively unstable, in the precise 4d sense that at least one scalar field sits at a maximum of the scalar potential and is therefore tachyonic, equivalently giving the slow-roll parameter eta_V < 0?

evidence.quote: The understanding of these solutions, built from all these works, has led to general beliefs that we formulate below as conjectures. Proving (or disproving) these conjectures has remained so far open problems, on which we report here.
Conjecture 2 Classical de Sitter solutions with intersecting sources are unstable.

We refer here to a classical, perturbative instability, different than a flat direction or even a metastable case that would be perturbatively stable. In a 4d language, this means that at least one 4d scalar field is at a maximum of its potential, i.e. tachyonic, implying for the standard slow-roll parameter eta_V < 0.

accepted.question_text: Can a classical de Sitter solution in this standard type-II-supergravity setting simultaneously satisfy all four conditions needed for a controlled string-theory origin - large internal volume, small string coupling, a bounded number of orientifolds, and quantized fluxes - or is such a simultaneous regime impossible for every classical de Sitter solution?
accepted.context_brief: String-origin control of de Sitter solutions

evidence.quote: The understanding of these solutions, built from all these works, has led to general beliefs that we formulate below as conjectures. Proving (or disproving) these conjectures has remained so far open problems, on which we report here.
Conjecture 3 Classical de Sitter solutions cannot have at the same time a large internal volume, a small string coupling, a bounded number of orientifolds and quantized fluxes.
This conjecture challenges the string origin of the solutions; as supergravity solutions, they remain valid and mathematically well-defined.

accepted.question_text: Let F be a free group of rank at least 2, and let H be a finitely generated subgroup of the direct product F x F. The membership problem for H in F x F asks for an algorithm that, given a word in the generators of F x F, decides whether that word represents an element of H. Does such an algorithm always exist for every finitely generated subgroup H of F x F?
accepted.context_brief: Membership in direct products of free groups

evidence.quote: The membership problem for a subgroup H <= G asks whether, given a word w in X union X^-1, it represents an element in H.
Question 5.17. Let F be a free group of rank >=2. Let H <= F x F be a finitely generated subgroup. Is the membership problem for H in F x F solvable?

accepted.question_text: Let G be a finitely presented group, and let H be a finitely generated subgroup of G whose membership problem in G is solvable, meaning there is an algorithm deciding whether a given word in G represents an element of H. Must the word problem in G itself then be solvable, that is, must there be an algorithm deciding whether a given word represents the identity element of G?

evidence.quote: Given a group G by a generating set X and a set of relators R, the word problem asks whether, given a word w in X union X^-1, it represents the trivial element in G.
The membership problem for a subgroup H <= G asks whether, given a word w in X union X^-1, it represents an element in H.
Question 5.18. Let G be a finitely presented group with a finitely generated subgroup H such that membership problem for H in G is solvable. Is the word problem in G solvable?

accepted.question_text: Suppose H is a hyperbolically embedded subgroup of G, meaning that there exists a relative presentation G = <X, H | R> for G with a strongly bounded relative presentation and a linear relative isoperimetric function. Let K be a finitely generated subgroup of H. If the membership problem for H in G is solvable, does it follow that the membership problem for K in G is also solvable?
accepted.context_brief: Membership transfer inside hyperbolically embedded subgroups

evidence.quote: Definition 4.6. A subgroup H <= G is hyperbolically embedded if there exists a relative presentation G = <X, H | R> for G and a constant C > 0 such that: (1) the relative presentation is strongly bounded; (2) the relative presentation has a linear relative isoperimetric function.
We denote by H <=h G a hyperbolically embedded subgroup.
Question 5.19. Suppose H <=h G, and that K <= H is a finitely generated subgroup. Is the membership problem for K in G solvable if the membership problem for H is solvable?
